title: Editing the animatic with sound in After Effects
content:
This is where the animatic comes together. In this part you'll bring the image sequences you rendered from Blender into After Effects, cut the shots together, then add sound: ambience, music and sound effects timed to the action, with their volume keyframed. A title and credits finish it. You'll need your rendered image sequences and some sounds you're allowed to use; the video uses After Effects 2020 on a Mac.

Bring in the image sequences

  1. Drag in each folder. 0:00 Start a blank After Effects project and drag the image sequence folders from Finder (or File Explorer) into the Project panel, one at a time: each comes in as a single piece of footage, not separate images.

  2. Rename each one after its folder. 0:30 The footage comes in named after its first and last images. Copy the folder's name, select the footage, press Return to rename it and paste.

  3. Set its frame rate to 24. 0:44 After Effects assumes image sequences are 30 frames per second, but Blender rendered them at 24. Right-click the footage and choose Interpret Footage → Main, then set Assume this frame rate to 24. The shortcut is Cmd+Option+G on a Mac (Ctrl+Alt+G on Windows) 2:38.

  4. Make the main composition. 1:14 Drag the footage down into the empty area at the bottom of the window, where the timeline will be: After Effects makes a new composition from it, at its size and frame rate. This is where you'll do all your editing.

  5. Or import them. 1:32 If you can't drag folders in, right-click in the Project panel and choose Import → File. Select the first image in a folder: PNG Sequence is ticked, so Open brings them all in as one sequence 1:56. Rename it and set it to 24 fps as before 2:21.

  6. Do the same for every sequence. 2:46 Drag in each folder, rename it and set it to 24 fps, until all the sequences are in 3:45.

Cut the shots together

  1. Make the composition long enough. 3:51 Choose Composition → Composition Settings and set Duration to about 20 seconds; six isn't enough 4:11.

  2. Trim a layer by dragging its ends. 4:18 Drag the start or end of a layer in the timeline to trim it. The footage you're not using still shows, ghosted, beyond the trimmed bar 4:32.

  3. Add the other shots and decide the cuts. 4:52 Drag in the other camera sequences. Turn on snapping, or press = over the timeline to zoom in, to place the playhead accurately 5:11. The layer on top shows, so trimming it switches the shot. Spread the layers out and reorder them 5:39: you're making editing decisions like any filmmaker given footage. Rough is fine for now 6:00.

  4. Split a shot by duplicating its layer. 7:10 To hold on a shot, cut away and come back, duplicate the layer (Cmd+D, or Ctrl+D on Windows), trim one copy before the cut and one after 7:17. Stacking them in time order shows the cascade of shots 7:24.

    After Effects can also split a layer at the playhead: Edit → Split Layer (Cmd+Shift+D, or Ctrl+Shift+D on Windows).

  5. Leave out what doesn't work. 8:15 One shot isn't used at all. The extra sequence rendered after the main animation, frames 144 to 192, goes at the end 8:38: a moment to take in that the dog has been taken. Its water bobs in a loop, so duplicating the layer a couple of times makes it last longer 9:07.

  6. Preview at full speed. 9:27 In the Preview panel, tick Cache Before Playback. Pressing play caches the whole timeline first, then plays it at the proper speed.

  7. Give it more time where it's rushed. 9:40 The middle went too fast. Drag-select the later layers (or Shift+click them in the layer list) and move them later 9:55. Line them up so there are no missing frames between them 10:46. The beam's cone makes the dog hard to see here: hiding it when rendering that scene would have helped 10:36.

Add sound

  1. Organize the project. 11:15 Right-click in the Project panel and make a New Folder called audio, and another, viewport-renders, for the image sequences.

  2. Find sounds you may use. 11:44 The music, "Space Residue" by Igor Amokian, comes from the Free Music Archive, browsed by genre. The sound effects come from freesound.org, where sounds are Creative Commons or public domain 12:10: an ambience of crickets and frogs by a river, a dog barking, a spaceship fly-by and a whoosh. Check each one's license, and note who to credit.

  3. Bring the audio in. 12:48 Drop the audio files into the Project panel and drag them into the audio folder. Add the ambience to the composition first; keep audio layers at the bottom of the timeline 13:16.

  4. Time a sound to the action with its waveform. 14:00 Twirl open an audio layer's Waveform to see where it gets loud. Trim the music and move it so its loud part lands right when the tractor beam comes down 14:27. If the shot is too short to see, move the footage layers to make room, then line the sound up with the cut 14:50; the blue line is the playhead 15:13.

  5. Keyframe the volume. 15:38 To make a sound fade out as the beam goes away, click the stopwatch beside Audio Levels to add a keyframe, move a frame or two on, and add another with the level dragged right down 15:43; here it's −54 dB. The arrows beside the property jump to the next or previous keyframe, so you don't have to line up the playhead yourself 17:04.

  6. Layer more sounds. 17:21 Sound effects make things feel as though they're making noise. The dog barking shouldn't go on after the dog is gone, so its level is keyframed down to nothing too 17:48.

Add a title

  1. Make room at the start. 18:29 Select all the layers and move them a few seconds later, leaving a gap at the beginning.

  2. Type the title. 18:39 Use the Type tool to write the title in the gap. Center it in the Paragraph panel 19:10, then select the layer and center it in the frame with the Align panel 19:19.

  3. Trim it and fade it in and out. 19:42 A new text layer runs the length of the timeline, so trim it to the gap. Twirl open its Transform properties 19:57 and keyframe Opacity: 0% at the start, 100% a moment later, then back to 0% at its end 20:03.

  4. Overlap the sound. 20:26 Starting a sound before its shot helps introduce what's coming. Here the ambience moves to the very beginning, under the title 20:47.

  5. Time the big moments. 21:05 Add a whoosh as the saucer flies away, lined up with the loud part of its waveform, and a bigger sound that's keyed down once the saucer has gone 22:09. Move it so it's loudest at the right moment, with keyframes so it doesn't start or stop abruptly, then fade it out 22:38. With the sounds layered and their levels tuned, it starts to feel like an animation 23:06.

Add credits

  1. Write the credits. 23:31 Use the Type tool again: something like "Animation by" and your name. Make it look less like a title, for example a lighter weight 24:06. As long as it's readable, it's up to you. Fade it in and out like the title.

  2. Overlap the credits with the last shot. 24:34 Have the credits fade in over the end of the last shot: overlapping helps tie shots together 24:47. Then fade the last footage layer out with Opacity keyframes so it doesn't stop abruptly 25:20.

  3. Check that every sound ends. 25:52 If a sound is still playing at the end, make sure its last Audio Levels keyframe is all the way down 26:01. If a fade ends too abruptly, add a keyframe in between 26:09.

26:22 The looping and timing could use more work, but it's good enough for an animatic. Next, you'll export it.
